brief.welcome: Welcome. You have joined %PRODUCT%, and the person who brought you here is about to work with you on it. This brief gives you, in order, the mission, the architecture, what is needed now and how to start; then the method, everything to read, and the rules. Take it in whole, tell your human what you understood, and the two of you can start.
brief.agent-file: You are in the %PRODUCT% repository. If the first message of this session is a task file's path (specs/tasks/<file>.xml), follow that file and nothing here. Otherwise read the brief, site/agents.xml in this checkout (the same as %SITE%agents.xml), and every file it lists, in its order; then tell your human what you understood before you change anything.
brief.page-note: For coding agents: the brief, agents.xml
brief.page-agent: Everything a coding agent needs to work on %PRODUCT% is in one place: the brief, %SITE%agents.xml. It explains what %PRODUCT% is and how it is built, lists every contribution open now, and leads to the spec, the rules and the task files, in the order to read them. Read it before you act on this page, and let your human choose what to do.
brief.intro: You were pointed here to understand %PRODUCT% or to help someone contribute to it. Read this brief whole, then the files it lists in the order given, then report back to your human before you change anything. Everything here is read from the repository (%REPO%, branch %BRANCH%); the files are the authority, this brief only orders them.
brief.prompt: Read %SITE%agents.xml and every file it lists, in its order. Then tell me, in your own words, what %PRODUCT% is, how it is built, and which open task or issue you think fits me; don't change anything yet.
brief.if-task-file: Stop reading this brief. A task file (specs/tasks/*.xml) is a complete instruction: follow its start element exactly. You may be in any session: build from the files alone, read whole in the method's order, and take nothing said earlier as authority. Nothing here adds to or overrides it.

architecture.note: How %PRODUCT% is put together, each part with the file that decides it. Read those files before you rely on any of this.
architecture.part: The process (the canvas, the MCP, turns and undo, the rules, the store) is shared by every database and names none of them. Everything about one database (its types, kinds, options, how it is read and written, its own tables) belongs to its engine: one crate, plugged in through one interface, checked by the conformance kit and the architecture check.

%PRODUCT% keeps its work in a PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector it bundles: one cluster per workspace, one database per schema. Each owner's tables are in its own namespace (cortex, workspace, engine_<id>, and a feature's own); every reference is a foreign key, every column documented in the database, and every rule a foreign key cannot state is enforced by the database at commit. Every change is an operation of a turn, logged, so it can be undone.

The cortex, the workspace, every engine and every feature is an owner: its own folder, card, namespace, rules, seeds and versions. A change adds; a rename takes two versions. A new engine or feature starts from the owner template.

specs/ holds the root (purpose, authority, method, sequence, decisions), the rules, this brief, the lessons and one task file per build. The spec is written before the code, and the code falls into it.

method.note: Every part of the product is built this way, by the maintainer and by every contributor, each with their own coding agent.
method.step: A person and an agent, with the maintainer, design or change the database in the owners' folders and write the work down as a task file under specs/tasks, every decision dated in specs/root.xml.

One agent, in any session, on a checkout of main, pointed at one task file and working from the files alone. It reads in the order the root gives, builds only what the file says, decides only what it lists, and stops when anything is missing or two files disagree, rather than guess.

step.name: gates
step.short: local · Docker · CI, in the PR

method.step: Every gate of the task file runs (local, Docker, CI), and their results go into the pull request.

step.name: review
step.short: a person merges; never the agent

method.step: A person reviews and merges; the agent never merges.
What a build taught is added to specs/lessons.xml, and a design session changes the method or the rules because of it. The method is open to improvement like the code.

way.name: build a wanted task
way.title: A task that is wanted
way.for-agent: Any task listed as wanted is open to everyone at once: your human points an agent, in any session, at the task file's path (specs/tasks/<file>.xml) on a fresh checkout of main; it builds from the files alone and opens the pull request under your human's GitHub account. Others may build the same task; the maintainer reviews the builds side by side and merges the best. It may be you, once you have read the files whole and set aside this conversation as authority.
way.for-people: Pick a task from the wanted list; nobody needs to assign it. On a fresh checkout of main, point your agent at the task file's path, in this session or a new one: it builds from the files alone. It reads, builds, runs the gates and opens the pull request; you review it, then submit. Others may build the same task: the maintainer merges the best, and what the builds teach improves the method.

way.name: bring something new
way.title: Something new
way.for-agent: An engine, a feature, a fix: for a new database, follow specs/guides/engine.xml from its first phase; otherwise your human opens an issue or a discussion; the design is agreed in a design session and written as a task file; then it is built as above.
way.for-people: An engine for a database you know (point your agent at the engine guide, specs/guides/engine.xml), a feature, a fix: open an issue or a discussion. You, your agent and the maintainer design it and write its task file; then it is built like any other.

way.name: improve the method
way.title: The way we work
way.for-agent: A lesson, a rule that would have caught a mistake, a clearer step: proposed in Discussions, decided in a design session.
way.for-people: A lesson from your build, a rule that would have caught a mistake, a clearer step: propose it in Discussions. The method is built in the open, like the code.

wanted.note: What is needed now, read from the root's sequence and decisions every time the brief is rendered.
wanted.ahead: Not written yet: the work after the queued tasks, each written as a task file once its decisions close. A feature you want to build may be here.
wanted.issues: Smaller work, fixes and questions are issues: %REPO%/issues, and the ones labelled good first issue are the place to begin.
wanted.ready: Written, and every task it depends on built. Anyone may build it; the best build is merged.
wanted.queued: Written, and waiting for the tasks before it: read it, and build it once they are merged.
wanted.design: Waiting for a design session with the maintainer: bring your view to Discussions.

first-steps.note: You do not need to know all of it to make a useful first contribution: your agent reads the project with you. Mistakes are caught before they land, in three ways: the checks every pull request runs (format, lint, every test, the architecture check and the spec check), the lock on the database's design, and a person's review. Each step below is small, real, and teaches something; building a task or an engine takes real skill, and these steps build it.
first-steps.step: Ask in Discussions how something works or why it was decided. It is answered in the open, so the next person finds it, and what confused you shows us where the docs are thin.

step.name: tell us what your agent understood

first-steps.step: Point your agent at this brief, then post what it explained back to you and where it was wrong. The brief is how every agent learns the project; your report tests it, and the fix helps every agent after yours.

Engines are proved against real schemas, not toy ones. A dump or hand-written schema of a database you know (schema only: no data, no secrets) becomes a sample every build of that engine must read and write back exactly. You learn where SQL hides its corners.

step.name: fix a page or a doc

first-steps.step: If a sentence took you two reads, it will take the next person two reads. Rewrite it in a pull request: pages and docs change like code, through the checks and a review, so you learn the whole path a change takes.

A task file is a complete instruction: what to build, its steps, its tests and the checks that decide. Give it to your agent in a fresh session, review what it builds, then submit. This is where you learn the method end to end; others may build the same task, and the best build is merged.

start.step: Read this brief whole, then the files of its reading list, in order.

Brief your human, in your own words and in a few minutes of reading: what %PRODUCT% is and why (the mission), how it is put together (the architecture), and where it stands (what is built, what is next).

Tell them they can start where they are, with you reading the project alongside them and the checks catching mistakes before they land, and show them the roster: the small first steps, then every contribution open now, one line each, from this brief's wanted list: the tasks ready to build, the tasks queued, the guides (a new engine), the decisions waiting for a design session, and the good first issues. For each: what it is, what it would teach them, and what it takes.

Let them pick what interests them. Tell them that anyone may take up the same task, that every build is reviewed side by side, and that the best one is merged: a build that is not merged still teaches, and its lesson improves the method.

To build a task: on a fresh checkout of main, point an agent at the task file's path, in any session; it builds from the files alone, and the pull request is opened under your own GitHub account. For a new database: the engine guide, from its first phase. For an issue or anything new: open the conversation on GitHub first, with your human's word.

read.note: Each group lists files; a group with a source takes its files from it: authority, the root's authority; sequence, the root's tasks in build order; guides, every guide of specs/guides; docs, every file of docs/ but the authority's.
read.group: identity and purpose, authority (which files decide), method (how every task is built), the sequence of tasks and every decision with its date
every rule, where it comes from, and what catches a breach

group.name: the task files, in the order they are built
the guides, one for each kind of contribution, read when you take one up
the design for people, read after the authority and never instead of it
the code as merged, when you need it

brief.database: Every table is a file of an owner's folder, one CREATE TABLE each, every column commented, its comments also in the database. Read a folder's files to know its tables; the owner template explains the shapes.

helping.do: Report what you understood first, in your own words, and ask your human what they want to do.
Start from an issue (%REPO%/issues, good first issue for a start) or a question in Discussions (%REPO%/discussions). Larger work is agreed with the maintainer before code, often as a task file.
Never change specs/, an owner's folder (schema/, engines/*/schema, features/), owner.toml or postgres/manifest.toml: they change only in a design session with the maintainer.
One issue, one branch, one pull request; tools/check.sh passes before you push (it needs Docker).
No attribution of any kind in commits or pull requests: your human is the author, and answers for every line.
Ask your human before you open an issue, push, comment or open a pull request: those speak for them.
